title: Pamela Snow on Blaming Parents for Children's Reading Struggles
author: Robert Pondiscio et al.
summary: Pondiscio republishes Pamela Snow's essay arguing that parents should not be blamed when children fail to learn to read. Snow's case rests on David Geary's distinction between biologically primary skills such as oral language and biologically secondary skills such as reading, which must be explicitly taught. She says Whole Language and Balanced Literacy rested on the false idea that reading is natural, enabling a folklore in education schools that shifted responsibility onto parents and away from teachers and systems. She lists what parents can usefully do, such as language-rich talk and reading aloud, but insists these are a bonus and not the mechanism of reading instruction. Her closing reframe is that schools should ask why a child is not progressing and how instruction can change.
points: Reading is a biologically secondary skill, so it needs explicit teaching and is primarily the school's responsibility.
Whole Language and Balanced Literacy rest on the mistaken premise that reading is natural, which let education faculties and schools sidestep teaching the writing code.
Blaming parents is a convenient excuse, and parental tutoring often hides the shortcomings of classroom instruction.
Parents help by building language, modelling reading and reading aloud, but this must not be mistaken for teaching reading.
The right question for schools is why a child is not progressing and how to adjust instruction.
quotes: There’s no shortage of odd, confusing, infuriating, ill-founded and contentious claims in education, and in the wider social chattersphere that sits around it, but surely there’s one that we can put to bed for good and for all: the idea that it is the job of parents to teach their children how to read
If reading was “natural”, we would not have hundreds of thousands of illiterate or semi-literate adults in the world (who, incidentally, in most cases, have been to school).
Biologically secondary skills, on the other hand, are skills that we humans have the capacity to learn but need to be taught.

Perhaps most perniciously, it meant that parents could be positioned as the primary agents of reading instruction, so that when children did not successfully become readers after three years of formal schooling, responsibility could be laid squarely at the feet of parents and the impugned quality of the home language and literacy environment.

Parents reading to their children should not be mistaken for the process by which children learn to read, any more than parents playing classical music to their children should be conflated with teaching them how to play a musical instrument.

The wrong question is the one directed at parents and is some version of “Do/did you read to her at home?” The right question for teachers and schools to ask is “Why is this child not progressing and how can we adjust our instruction to address this”?
